macro.title: What It Means — VWRA, Bonds, Gold & BTC

reads.label: VWRA (held)
reads.text: eased to ~$185 as global equities mark time; the swing is not the Fed but Microsoft and Meta after Wednesday’s bell — their AI-capex guidance moves a world index more than 25 basis points would.

reads.label: Global bonds (held)
reads.text: the 10-year barely moved at 4.62%; a hold-and-hawkish statement is the base case, an out-of-consensus hike the tail.

reads.label: Gold (read only)
reads.text: near $4,030 and soft on the firmer dollar — and the honest correction: it sits roughly 15 per cent below January’s ~$4,736 record, so “near a record” no longer fits.

reads.label: Bitcoin (read only)
reads.text: below $64k, trading as high-beta risk on the stronger dollar, not as gold’s twin. The two he holds stay VWRA and global bonds; the two he only reads stay gold and BTC.

stories.headline: Five Quiet Days, and the Barrel Still Sells
stories.dek: The pause held into a fifth day as Iran, Saudi Arabia and Oman talked the Strait in Muscat and Washington talked up a deal. Still no signature on the twin-corridor draft — and Brent slid again to $84, its lowest in over a week. The tape is pricing the peace faster than anyone will sign it.

stories.headline: Certified Fresh, and Swinging Into Singapore Tomorrow
stories.dek: The embargo No. 55 was waiting on has lifted, and the number exists: Spider-Man: Brand New Day is Certified Fresh at 91 per cent — the best-reviewed Marvel film since Shang-Chi, and the weakest of Tom Holland’s four solos. It opens here Wednesday, tracking as the biggest debut of 2026. The verdict landed; the box office has not.

stories.kicker: The Macro Desk · The Portfolio Lens
stories.headline: Everything Waits for Warsh
stories.dek: The board went quiet before it goes loud. Oil kept sliding and the dollar firmed to a four-week high, but equities, gold and bitcoin all marked time — because the week’s real events land after this issue does: the Fed’s first decision under Kevin Warsh tonight, and Microsoft and Meta’s earnings after the bell. Market explanation, not investment advice.

stories.headline: The Bank Banks Twenty Billion, and Doubles Down
stories.dek: Two days after tightening when the Street had pencilled in a hold, the Monetary Authority of Singapore posted a S$20 billion profit — and used the same week to signal the squeeze is not finished. Core inflation is set to step up from this month, the output gap is now seen widening, and October is the date to watch.

stories.headline: The First Wall Comes Down
stories.dek: For the first time since the market turned, a cooling measure has been unwound. The government has scrapped the fifteen-month wait a private-home owner faced before buying an HDB resale flat — effective at once — and given en-bloc developers up to two more years to sell. Loosening, not tightening, is now the direction of travel.

stories.headline: Open Weights, With Strings Attached
stories.dek: The biggest open model ever released turns out to be open with an asterisk: Kimi K3 ships under a custom licence, not a free one, and its own benchmark charts quietly left out a hallucination rate above fifty per cent. Behind it, the harder sovereignty number lands — Nvidia’s China share said to have fallen from forty per cent to eight in a year.

stories.headline: Sony Dates Its RAW Cine Body
stories.dek: The FX5 is official and priced — US$4,898 for the body, shipping mid-August, with 5K Open Gate and internal 16-bit RAW, the first Cinema Line under BURANO to record it. Above it, Samsung breaks its price silence on the Galaxy Glasses without quite naming a number; below, Garmin buys the software the endurance crowd already trains on.

stories.headline: A Wikipedia of Devices, Built From the Houses Themselves
stories.dek: Home Assistant’s Open Home Foundation opened its Device Database to the public this week — a searchable record of what actually works, built not from one-time lab certification but from anonymised data flowing out of real homes. Two thousand devices in, it answers the only question a migrator ever asks: will this thing work with mine?

stories.headline: Bond’s Car, Rebuilt on the Wrist
stories.dek: Breitling and Aston Martin have turned the DB5 — the most famous car in cinema — into a trio of chronographs, down to a wooden ring that echoes the steering wheel and subdials shaped like the dashboard gauges. From US$11,400 to $41,500, it is a beautiful piece of film memorabilia, and the honest question is how much of the price is the watch and how much is the movie.

stories.headline: The Lever Isn’t the Screen. It’s the Legs.
stories.dek: Amid a year of headlines about what to take away from children, a large UK cohort study points at something to add. Movement measured on the wrist at age seven predicted fewer emotional and peer problems at eleven and fourteen — an argument for the pitch and the playground, not just the parental-controls menu. General guidance, not medical advice.

stories.headline: A Rocky World, 48 Light-Years Off, Is Leaking Helium
stories.dek: Astronomers have confirmed the first atmosphere on a rocky planet in a star’s habitable zone — not by seeing air, but by catching helium escaping the top of it. The world is a super-Earth around a red dwarf, and the surprise is not that it might be alive. It is that a small rocky planet kept its air at all.

stories.headline: The Quiet Collapse of the Close Friend
stories.dek: The dating recession has a companion statistic, and it is starker. The share of American men with no close friends rose fivefold in a generation — from 3 per cent to 15 — as the informal machinery that used to manufacture friendship quietly shut down. For a reader in his mid-40s, it is the relationship trend that matters most and gets discussed least.

stories.headline: Much Ado About Zone 2
stories.dek: The most fashionable idea in midlife fitness — that slow, below-threshold cardio is uniquely magic for the mitochondria — is getting a careful walking-back. Match the total work and harder intervals do as much or more, and for anyone training under six hours a week, intensity is simply the better use of the time. Not medical advice.

stories.headline: The Autumn Calendar Firms Up
stories.dek: The concert diary hardens into real decisions — The Weeknd’s tickets are already out, the Grand Prix adds a Sprint and a stadium-grade bill — while the seats worth setting an alarm for open next week.

stories.headline: The Battle Fought After the Peace
stories.dek: On 8 January 1815, British and American armies met at New Orleans and left two thousand casualties on the field. The war they were fighting had already ended — a peace signed in Ghent two weeks earlier, still crossing the Atlantic by sail. For most of history the deadly gap sat between an event and the news of it. We spent two centuries closing that gap. Then we did something stranger.
